extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional design, and comparative history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and assesses principles and institutional criteria for stable (or unstable) constitutions and balances of power, illustrated by historical cases (Venice, United Provinces, England, Poland). Useful for judging institutional design and constitutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of voting in assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: The people still maintained their right of voting in assembly, which was a great privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserving the formal right of popular assembly vote is treated as an important constitutional safeguard; loss or erosion of this right marks a shift toward aristocratic domination (example: Venice where people at first retained voting rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid electoral mechanisms that nullify popular power
rubrics_metrics.description: Not perceiving that this law would be fatal to their power, suffered that aristocracy to be thus founded, which subsists to this hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect, multi-stage selection processes (or other legal contrivances) that appear to preserve election but effectively remove real influence from the people are criticised as fatal to popular power (example: staged elector/ grand council system in Venice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive orders require concurring council (checks on executive)
rubrics_metrics.description: No orders should be valid without their concurrence (privy council of six for the doge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instituting a small council whose concurrence is required for executive orders is given as a measure to restrain an unchecked chief magistrate (example: a privy council of six appointed for the doge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of administrative officers from the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand council thought it improper that the public acts should be signed by chancellors appointed by [the doge], and accordingly determined to appoint this officer themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointment of key administrative officers by a body other than the executive reduces executive patronage and concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hereditary or life-tenure legislative seats (prevent aristocratic entrenchment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law that all the members of the grand council should hold their places for life, and transmit them to their posterity... This establishment of a hereditary legislative nobility shocked the citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making legislative membership permanent and transmissible to descendants entrenches oligarchy and undermines popular representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-term inquiry and financial accountability for executives
rubrics_metrics.description: Six new magistrates, called correctors, were created... to inquire into all abuses during the reign of a deceased doge, and report them to the senate; it was enacted, that the fortune of the doge should indemnify the state for whatever damage it had suffered during his administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms for retrospective inquiry and state indemnification by an executive's personal fortune are proposed as accountability measures to deter abuse of office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex multi-stage ballot to limit factional control
rubrics_metrics.description: A complicated mixture of choice and chance: successive ballots with gilt and white balls reduce the body to a small set of electors who finally elect the doge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layered, partly random, multi-stage electoral procedures are described as institutional devices intended to break factional dominance and prevent manipulation of a single electoral body (detailed Venetian ballot process provided as model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against bribery and purchase of acclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: The new-chosen doge, having taken care to distribute money among the multitude, was received with universal acclamations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral corruption via distribution of money or largess undermines legitimacy; the text treats bribery and public largess to secure acclamation as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual checks between courts and councils (balanced powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great care is taken... to balance one court against another, and render their powers mutual checks to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designing institutions so that different councils/courts check one another (composition and overlapping competences) is presented as a core principle for durable government (examples: seigniory composition and addition of chambers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict and impartial execution of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A punctual execution of the laws, is no doubt essential to the existence of this state; there are striking instances of persons punishing their nearest relations, with the most unrelenting severity; without this, the doge... or the people... would soon think of an union against the ruling nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent, impartial enforcement of laws (even against relatives) is argued to be necessary to preserve order and prevent conspiracies against the ruling regime; presented as both a virtue and a tool of regime stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and danger) of secret tribunals and state inquisitors
rubrics_metrics.description: The state inquisitors... decide, without appeal, on the life of every citizen... They employ what spies they please; if unanimous, they may order a prisoner to be strangled in gaol, or drowned in the canal... They may command access to the house of every individual... By this tribunal have doge, nobility, and people, been kept in awe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret, extra-judicial organs can be effective instruments of control and deterrence but are described as terrifying and arbitrary; the passage functions as both explanation of how Venice preserved its aristocracy and a caution about such mechanisms' oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation into three powers/orders for balance
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be, in the nature of things, no balance without three powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts that a stable balance requires three distinct powers (e.g., executive, aristocratic assembly, popular assembly/representation); neglecting this tri-partite balance leads to dominance by one order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open offices by law to men of merit (avoid exclusive family privileges)
rubrics_metrics.description: They have never had any exclusive preferences of families or nobles. Offices have, by law at least, been open to all men of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal openness of offices to competent individuals (merit-based access) reduces aristocratic monopoly and promotes a more equitable and capable administration (example: United Provinces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable representation in the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people are not equitably represented in the house of commons, this is a departure in practice from the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative assemblies must reflect the people equitably; failure to do so is identified as a departure from constitutional theory and a potential source of imbalance (applies to England/America comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive veto/negative on legislature as a balancing device
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have not indeed imitated it in giving a negative, upon their legislature to the executive power; in this respect their balances are incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legislative negative (veto) vested in the executive is discussed as one mechanism to complete the system of checks and balances; absence of such a negative may leave the balance incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal, constitutional, and peaceable modes for changing rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary, to avoid continual violence, to give the people a legal, constitutional, and peaceable mode of changing these rulers, whenever they discover improper principles or dispositions in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should provide lawful, peaceful procedures for replacing rulers to avoid recurrent violent uprisings; this is praised as both prudent and necessary, notably for American contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated statutory limits on executive/kingly powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The king... has not the power to make laws, raise taxes, contract alliances, or declare war, nor to coin money, nor marry, without the ratification of the diet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit constitutional constraints (e.g., requiring legislative ratification for taxes, laws, alliances, war, coinage, marriage) are presented as mechanisms that limit executive arbitrariness (example: Polish limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of the third estate/people in representative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate is composed of the clergy and nobility; the third estate, or people, is not so much as known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to include commoners or the 'third estate' in political decision-making is criticized as producing imbalance and oligarchic domination; inclusion of the people is necessary for a balanced constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular assemblies and oath-bound conditions constraining rulers (pacta conventa)
rubrics_metrics.description: A charter, called pacta conventa... contained... that the king should be elective; that diets be assembled every two years; that every nobleman... should have a vote in the diet of election; that if the king should infringe the laws and privileges of the nation, his subjects should be absolved from their oaths of allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal, pre-election contractual constraints on rulers (regular assemblies, electoral rules, enforceable oaths and conditions) are instruments to bind sovereigns and protect constitutional order (Polish pacta conventa as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralized judiciary and transfer of supreme jurisdiction undermine central authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking from the king the supreme jurisdiction of the causes of the nobles... each palatinate shall elect in their dietines their own judges, who shall form supreme courts of justice... in which the causes of the nobles shall be decided without appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting autonomous judicial powers to localities and removing appellate central jurisdiction from the sovereign can fragment authority and contribute to disorder or oligarchic power; treated as a 'fatal blow' to prerogative in Poland.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venality and purchase of crowns corrodes constitutional legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every succeeding king... has always been constrained to purchase the crown by a public largess, and private corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systemic bribery and the buying of office or throne are condemned as causes of corruption and degeneration of constitutional systems (example: Polish elections where candidates buy votes with largesses and bribes).
